screens.title: Performance Optimization in Unity
screens.narratorSegment: Performance starts with measurement. In this lesson you will learn how to use the Unity Profiler to find the real bottlenecks in C P U, G P U, and memory, and then apply focused fixes in scripting, rendering, assets, and physics. We'll examine common C# pitfalls that cause garbage collection spikes, practical patterns to reuse memory and cache components, and rendering techniques like static batching, dynamic batching, and G P U instancing to reduce draw calls. You will also learn asset best practices: texture compression, mipmaps, and atlases. Finally we'll cover physics optimizations such as configuring the collision matrix, adjusting the fixed timestep, and allowing rigidbodies to sleep. Each optimization is an iterative step: profile first, change one thing, then profile again. A concrete example you will revisit is a CubeSpawner script that initially causes GC allocations and many draw calls; we will refactor it to reduce allocations and enable instancing. By the end you will know how to find the biggest gains and avoid wasting time on premature micro-optimizations. What will you fix first when you open the Profiler?

screens.title: Why profile first
screens.narratorSegment: Profiling is the first step in any optimization workflow because it tells you where time and memory are actually spent. Guessing leads to wasted effort and sometimes regressions. Unity's Profiler shows C P U usage broken down by scripts, rendering, physics, and other systems. It also reports G P U timings, memory allocations, audio costs, and the GC Alloc counter that reveals how often your code is allocating new managed objects. A good profile session starts with a representative playthrough and a recording of the Profiler timeline. Look for tall spikes and persistent sections that consume many milliseconds per frame. Note which functions or systems show the largest cost. For example, a frequent small allocation inside Update will appear as repeated GC Alloc samples and often aligns with micro-stutters. Another common pattern is many small draw calls listed in the Rendering section. The key workflow is: profile, pick the biggest offender, change one thing, and re-profile. This repeatable loop prevents chasing low-impact changes. A common misconception is to optimize everything at once; instead, focus on the single change that yields the largest measurable improvement and verify it by comparing before and after metrics.

content.html:
Core Concept
Why profile first
A clear definition, example, and verification loop.
Definition: The Profiler records where your frame time and allocations go so you can target real bottlenecks.
Example: A GC Alloc spike every second corresponds to a string concatenation in Update; the Profiler points to that method.
Common mistake: Optimizing without a profile often wastes time on low-impact code paths.
Key Takeaway

Always profile a representative scene, change only one variable at a time, and re-measure to confirm improvement.

Profiler checklist
  • Record a typical play session to capture representative behavior.
  • Inspect CPU, Rendering, Memory, and GC Alloc for repeated patterns.
  • Pinpoint the highest-cost functions and systems first.
  • Apply one optimization and re-run the profile to verify gains.
Quick analogy
Profiling is like using a thermometer: you wouldn't treat a fever without measuring temperature first.

screens.title: Interpreting Profiler panels
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the main Profiler panels helps you quickly form a hypothesis about the cause of poor performance. The C P U panel shows where frame time is spent: look for long bars and which systems or functions dominate. The Rendering section lists draw calls and can reveal many small separate draws that add C P U overhead. The Memory view shows total memory use and allocations; frequent small allocations show up as rising GC Alloc values and eventual garbage collection events. The G P U section reports G P U cost; if the G P U is the bottleneck, reducing fill rate or shader complexity may help. A useful process is to capture a short profile, find the highest-cost sample, then open the detailed view for that sample to see the call stack. For example, if Update functions show high cost, examine your scripts for new allocations or expensive operations in high-frequency methods. If Rendering shows many draw calls, investigate materials and whether objects share materials so they can batch. Finally, use the timeline to correlate spikes across panels to identify cause and effect: a GC Alloc surge followed by a C P U spike often indicates a GC pause.

content.html:
Process Flow
Interpreting Profiler panels
Use a short capture and correlate spikes across panels.
CPU: Identify heavy Update/LateUpdate work and expensive GetComponent or allocation patterns.
Rendering: Count draw calls and check for repeated material switches that break batching.
Memory: Watch GC Alloc; repeated small allocations lead to frequent GC events and hitches.
GPU: If the GPU time dominates, check shaders, overdraw, and texture formats.
Step-by-step timeline analysis
  1. Record a 10–20 second session of representative gameplay.
  2. Find a big spike in the Timeline view.
  3. Open the detailed sample to view the call stack and memory allocations.
  4. Form a targeted hypothesis and implement one change.
  5. Re-run the profile and compare metrics to confirm improvement.
Common misconception

A single poor frame doesn't necessarily indicate a steady bottleneck; verify with repeated captures and representative input.

screens.title: C# scripting best practices
screens.narratorSegment: C# scripting patterns determine whether your code makes frequent allocations or performs expensive lookups every frame. The most impactful practices are: cache component references, avoid allocations inside Update or LateUpdate, reuse data structures, and use StringBuilder for repeated string assembly. Caching means calling GetComponent in Awake or Start and storing the reference in a private field for later use. Avoid creating new lists or new strings in per-frame code. Instead, clear and reuse a pre-allocated List, or use pooled objects for frequently created GameObjects. Reusing a Vector3 instance reduces frequent struct-to-object operations in code that sets positions often. StringBuilder prevents repeated string concatenation from allocating new strings. A misconception is that small allocations are harmless; in aggregate they can cause many GC cycles that produce micro-stutters. Start by finding allocations flagged in the Profiler, then apply these patterns to the specific method identified. The goal isn't zero allocation initially, but to remove repeated allocations from high-frequency paths. C# scripting best practices means cache and reuse objects; avoid 'new' inside update and prefer pre-allocated structures.. In practical terms, patterns that reduce cpu cost and gc pressure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
C# scripting best practices

Practical rules to reduce allocation and runtime cost.

Cache GetComponent results in Awake or Start instead of calling it in Update.
Reuse lists and arrays: clear and refill instead of creating new collections every frame.
Use StringBuilder for repeated string building to avoid allocations.
Reuse Vector3 instances when updating many positions each frame.
Example patterns
Caching: store Rigidbody or Renderer in a private field during Awake.
Reuse list: call list.Clear() and add items instead of new List each time.
Common mistake

Putting allocations, expensive reflection, or GetComponent calls inside Update causes repeated cost that adds up quickly.

screens.title: Avoiding allocations: Vector3 and GetComponent
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through two common anti-patterns and their optimized alternatives. First, creating a new position Vector3 on every Update call. Allocating a new object or temporary struct repeatedly can cause unnecessary work and, in some contexts, allocations that contribute to GC or C P U overhead. Instead, cache a Vector3 field and modify its components each frame before assigning it to transform. position. Second, calling GetComponent inside Update repeatedly is expensive. It may not directly allocate managed memory, but it causes C P U work and can indirectly cause allocations when accessing properties like material, which can create copies. The best practice is to call GetComponent in Awake or Start, store the component in a private field, and use that field in Update. Below you'll see the original and optimized snippets. Read the optimized version, note the cached fields in Awake, and see how Update becomes a lightweight update of existing references. A common misconception is that small refactors like this are unnecessary; for high-frequency code they are often the difference between smooth gameplay and micro-stutters. Avoiding allocations: Vector3 and GetComponent means modify cached structures and cached component references instead of creating new objects per frame.. In practical terms, real code examples and safer patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Vector3 allocation fix
Original code creates new Vector3 every frame; optimized code reuses a cached Vector3.
// Common mistake: Allocating new Vector3 every frame
void Update()
{
    transform.position = new Vector3(transform.position.x + Speed * Time.deltaTime,
                                     transform.position.y,
                                     transform.position.z);
}

// Optimized: Reusing a cached Vector3
private Vector3 _cachedPosition;

void Awake()
{
    _cachedPosition = transform.position;
}

void Update()
{
    _cachedPosition.x += Speed * Time.deltaTime;
    transform.position = _cachedPosition;
}
Caching GetComponent
GetComponent inside Update often costs CPU. Cache it in Awake and use the cached reference.
// Common mistake: GetComponent in Update
void Update()
{
    GetComponent().AddForce(Vector3.up * JumpForce);
}

// Optimized: Caching the component reference
private Rigidbody _rb;

void Awake()
{
    _rb = GetComponent();
}

void Update()
{
    if (Input.GetButtonDown("Jump"))
    {
        _rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * JumpForce);
    }
}
Key Takeaway

These simple changes reduce per-frame CPU cost and avoid patterns that often align with GC or rendering overhead.

screens.title: Refactor CubeSpawner to reduce GC Alloc
screens.narratorSegment: The CubeSpawner example is a practical way to see GC allocations in the Profiler and practice refactoring. The unoptimized Update used string concatenation each second to log a message, which creates temporary strings and contributes to allocations. The optimized version uses a single StringBuilder instance stored in a private field. Each time we want to log, we clear the builder, append pieces, and call ToString for a single managed allocation. This pattern significantly reduces allocations when logging frequently. The Start method shows heavy work during instantiation; instantiating a thousand cubes at once is expected to cost C P U, but you can reduce runtime cost by ensuring all cubes share the same material and by enabling G P U instancing. Also, avoid calling GetComponent or accessing material properties that create copies while setting up many objects. After the refactor, run the Profiler and compare the GC Alloc column before and after. You'll typically see the GC allocations drop, fewer GC events, and a smoother frame timeline. content.html:
Hands-on Activity
CubeSpawner improvements
Replace per-frame string concatenation with a single StringBuilder instance and reuse it for periodic logs.
using UnityEngine;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public class CubeSpawner : MonoBehaviour
{
    public GameObject cubePrefab;
    public int numberOfCubes = 1000;
    public float spawnRadius = 50f;

    // Optimized update: use a single StringBuilder
    private System.Text.StringBuilder _stringBuilder = new System.Text.StringBuilder();

    void Start()
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < numberOfCubes; i++)
        {
            Vector3 randomPos = transform.position + Random.insideUnitSphere * spawnRadius;
            GameObject newCube = Instantiate(cubePrefab, randomPos, Quaternion.identity);
            // Ensure all cubes use the same material to enable batching/instancing
        }
    }

    void Update()
    {
        if (Time.frameCount % 60 == 0)
        {
            _stringBuilder.Clear();
            _stringBuilder.Append("Current frame: ").Append(Time.frameCount).Append(" - ").Append(Random.value);
            Debug.Log(_stringBuilder.ToString());
        }
    }
}
Practical verification
Run the scene with the Profiler open. Note GC Alloc and CPU spikes before change. After switching to StringBuilder and reusing lists, the GC Alloc samples should reduce and pauses should disappear or shrink.
Key Takeaway

Minimizing temporary objects in high-frequency code paths leads to large runtime gains.

screens.title: Draw calls and rendering cost
screens.narratorSegment: A draw call is the C P U telling the G P U to render a set of triangles with a given material and state. Each draw call has C P U overhead, so many separate draws increase C P U time even if the G P U work per draw is small. Reducing draw calls reduces the number of times the G P U state must change and can dramatically lower C P U render time. Typical strategies include static batching, which combines multiple static meshes that share a material into one mesh; dynamic batching, which merges small moving meshes under strict vertex limits; and G P U instancing, which tells the G P U to draw many instances of the same mesh with one call while allowing per-instance data like transforms or colors passed via shader buffers. A common beginner mistake is changing materials per-object will break batching. If you need unique colors, use Material Property Blocks or instancing rather than unique materials. Always verify in the Rendering profiler: you should see draw call counts drop after enabling batching or instancing. The largest wins usually come from changing many objects so they can share materials and thereby participate in batching or instancing.

A common beginner mistake is changing materials per-object will break batching. If you need unique colors, use Material Property Blocks or instancing rather than unique materials. Always verify in the Rendering profiler: you should see draw call counts drop after enabling batching or instancing. keyIdea.title: Reduce draw calls
keyIdea.text: Make many objects share materials or use instancing so the CPU issues fewer render commands.

content.html:
Core Concept
Draw calls and rendering cost
Definition: A draw call is a CPU command that tells the GPU to render geometry with a specific material and state.
Why it matters: Each draw call adds CPU overhead; many small draws produce higher CPU time than fewer large draws.
Static batching: best for non-moving objects that share materials.
Dynamic batching: best for many small moving meshes that meet vertex limits.
GPU instancing: best for many copies of the same mesh with per-instance data.
Concrete example
Hundreds of identical trees using the same material are a perfect fit for GPU instancing. If each tree has its own material, batching breaks and draw calls remain high. Enabling instancing or using a shared material collapses hundreds of draws into one or a few.
Common misconception

Marking everything as static guarantees the best performance. Not always: static batching increases build size and only applies to objects that do not move.

screens.title: Static vs Dynamic Batching
screens.narratorSegment: Static and dynamic batching both aim to reduce draw calls but work in different scenarios. Static batching combines multiple non-moving meshes that share a material into a single large mesh at build or runtime for fewer draw calls. It is very effective for environment geometry that never moves, but it increases memory and build-time processing. Dynamic batching attempts to merge small moving meshes at runtime, but it has strict limits on vertex count and shader properties; too many vertices or complex vertex data prevent dynamic batching. G P U instancing is often a better alternative when you have many similar moving objects because instancing handles large counts efficiently and allows per-instance variation via shader buffers or Material Property Blocks. A common pitfall is expecting dynamic batching to handle large or complex meshes; it cannot. Choose static batching for many static objects, dynamic batching only for small simple moving objects, and instancing when you need many copies with variation. Always verify in the Profiler's Rendering panel to ensure your chosen approach reduced draw calls. Static batching
Best for non-moving meshes that share materials. Reduces draw calls strongly but increases build-time and combined mesh memory.
When to use: Terrain pieces, environment props, objects that never move.
Dynamic batching
Merges small moving meshes at runtime under vertex limits. It’s automatic but limited by vertex count and shader complexity.
When to use: Many small characters or projectiles with simple shaders.

For hundreds of similar objects, GPU instancing usually outperforms dynamic batching and supports per-instance variation.

screens.title: Asset optimization: textures and atlases
screens.narratorSegment: Textures are often the largest contributor to memory and load times. screens.title: Physics optimization strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Physics can be a hidden C P U cost in complex simulations. A few targeted settings yield large savings. First, use the layer-based collision matrix in Project Settings to disable collisions between layers that never need to interact. This reduces the number of pairwise checks dramatically. Second, tune the Fixed Timestep: a smaller timestep increases physics accuracy but raises C P U cost; a larger timestep reduces cost at the expense of fidelity. Find a balance that preserves gameplay feel. Third, allow rigidbodies to sleep when idle so they don't participate in expensive checks unnecessarily. Unity automatically handles sleeping, but your interactions should avoid constantly waking sleeping bodies. Fourth, prefer simple primitive colliders—box, sphere, capsule—over non-convex mesh colliders where possible because mesh colliders are much more expensive. Lastly, remove colliders from objects that will never participate in collisions and use kinematic bodies appropriately. After making changes, profile the physics section and observe reduced C P U time for Physics. FixedUpdate and fewer collision checks. Process Flow
Physics optimization strategies
Layer-based collision: disable unnecessary layer interactions in Project Settings → Physics to cut collision checks.
Fixed Timestep: increase timestep to reduce physics frequency, balancing accuracy and CPU cost.

Example scenario
If you have many projectiles that should not hit each other, place them on a dedicated layer and disable collisions between projectile instances. This reduces pair checks and improves physics throughput.

Tune physics settings to the needs of your gameplay; fewer interactions and simpler colliders often deliver big wins.

fullNarratorScript:
Performance starts with measurement. In this lesson you will learn how to use the Unity Profiler to find the real bottlenecks in C P U, G P U, and memory, and then apply focused fixes in scripting, rendering, assets, and physics. We'll examine common C# pitfalls that cause garbage collection spikes, practical patterns to reuse memory and cache components, and rendering techniques like static batching, dynamic batching, and G P U instancing to reduce draw calls. You will also learn asset best practices: texture compression, mipmaps, and atlases. Finally we'll cover physics optimizations such as configuring the collision matrix, adjusting the fixed timestep, and allowing rigidbodies to sleep. Each optimization is an iterative step: profile first, change one thing, then profile again. A concrete example you will revisit is a CubeSpawner script that initially causes GC allocations and many draw calls; we will refactor it to reduce allocations and enable instancing. By the end you will know how to find the biggest gains and avoid wasting time on premature micro-optimizations. What will you fix first when you open the Profiler?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to use Unity's Profiler to find performance hotspots in C P U, G P U, and memory, and then apply precise fixes. You will learn C# scripting patterns that reduce garbage collection by caching components, reusing collections, and avoiding allocations inside Update loops. You will be able to reduce draw calls through static and dynamic batching and enable G P U instancing where appropriate. You will also optimize assets by choosing the right texture compression, enabling mipmaps, and using texture atlases to help batching. Finally, you will configure physics settings: use the layer-based collision matrix, choose a suitable fixed timestep, and remove unnecessary colliders so simulations run efficiently. Each objective ties measurement to action so you focus effort where it matters. You will practice these skills with a CubeSpawner example that demonstrates profiling, refactoring to use StringBuilder and cached components, and enabling instancing to cut draw calls. These are practical, repeatable skills you can apply to your own projects.

These practical objectives focus on actions you can perform in a test scene. First, you will create a PerformanceTest scene and run the Profiler while spawning many objects to generate measurable load. Second, you will refactor a CubeSpawner script: switch string concatenation to a StringBuilder, cache Rigidbody or Renderer references in Awake, and reuse collections rather than allocating new ones each frame. Third, you will enable G P U instancing on a shared material and mark static objects to exploit static batching when appropriate. Fourth, you will inspect texture import settings—enable suitable compression, generate mipmaps, and consider atlases for many small textures. Each objective includes a verification step: run the Profiler, record C P U and GC Alloc peaks, apply a single optimization, and compare the new metrics. This practice shows you how to tie code changes to measurable improvements and avoids premature optimization by focusing on high-impact fixes.

Profiling is the first step in any optimization workflow because it tells you where time and memory are actually spent. Guessing leads to wasted effort and sometimes regressions. Unity's Profiler shows C P U usage broken down by scripts, rendering, physics, and other systems. It also reports G P U timings, memory allocations, audio costs, and the GC Alloc counter that reveals how often your code is allocating new managed objects. A good profile session starts with a representative playthrough and a recording of the Profiler timeline. Look for tall spikes and persistent sections that consume many milliseconds per frame. Note which functions or systems show the largest cost. For example, a frequent small allocation inside Update will appear as repeated GC Alloc samples and often aligns with micro-stutters. Another common pattern is many small draw calls listed in the Rendering section. The key workflow is: profile, pick the biggest offender, change one thing, and re-profile. This repeatable loop prevents chasing low-impact changes. A common misconception is to optimize everything at once; instead, focus on the single change that yields the largest measurable improvement and verify it by comparing before and after metrics.

Understanding the main Profiler panels helps you quickly form a hypothesis about the cause of poor performance. The C P U panel shows where frame time is spent: look for long bars and which systems or functions dominate. The Rendering section lists draw calls and can reveal many small separate draws that add C P U overhead. The Memory view shows total memory use and allocations; frequent small allocations show up as rising GC Alloc values and eventual garbage collection events. The G P U section reports G P U cost; if the G P U is the bottleneck, reducing fill rate or shader complexity may help. A useful process is to capture a short profile, find the highest-cost sample, then open the detailed view for that sample to see the call stack. For example, if Update functions show high cost, examine your scripts for new allocations or expensive operations in high-frequency methods. If Rendering shows many draw calls, investigate materials and whether objects share materials so they can batch. Finally, use the timeline to correlate spikes across panels to identify cause and effect: a GC Alloc surge followed by a C P U spike often indicates a GC pause.

C# scripting patterns determine whether your code makes frequent allocations or performs expensive lookups every frame. The most impactful practices are: cache component references, avoid allocations inside Update or LateUpdate, reuse data structures, and use StringBuilder for repeated string assembly. Caching means calling GetComponent in Awake or Start and storing the reference in a private field for later use. Avoid creating new lists or new strings in per-frame code. Instead, clear and reuse a pre-allocated List, or use pooled objects for frequently created GameObjects. Reusing a Vector3 instance reduces frequent struct-to-object operations in code that sets positions often. StringBuilder prevents repeated string concatenation from allocating new strings. A misconception is that small allocations are harmless; in aggregate they can cause many GC cycles that produce micro-stutters. The goal isn't zero allocation initially, but to remove repeated allocations from high-frequency paths. Textures are often the largest contributor to memory and load times. Choose an appropriate compression format for your target platform; this reduces memory and G P U bandwidth usage. Enable mipmaps for textures that will be seen at different distances so the G P U can sample lower-resolution versions for distant objects and reduce aliasing and fill rate. These key concepts capture the most actionable ideas from this chapter. Third, reduce draw calls by sharing materials, using static batching for fixed geometry, and using G P U instancing for many similar moving objects; Material Property Blocks let you vary instances without creating new materials. Fifth, tune physics with the collision matrix, fixed timestep adjustments, and simple colliders.
